Introduction:

Nested Library Analysis (NLA) was proposed by Huang et al. 2024: Detecting shifts in nonlinear dynamics using Empirical Dynamic Modeling with Nested-Library Analysis.

Note

NLA is intended to answer this research question:

Does the variable of interest present any change point in time?

In brief, NLA steps are:

1 To use time series data to reconstruct the system’s dynamics (via EDM),

2. To gradually remove older data (“shrinking the library”), and

3. To find the point where prediction accuracy improves the most.

That point corresponds to a regime shift, because older data comes from a different dynamical regime and actually harms prediction.

Huang et al. 2024 found that NLA is capable to detect change points and outperforms existing approaches based on statistical characteristics. Indeed, Huang et al. 2024 work shows that shifts in mean and variance cannot serve as a generic signal of regime shifts.

NLA repository associated to the original publication is stored here.

In this notebook we want to:

Important

We want:

  • to replace S-map with (Gaussian Process Empirical Dynamic Modelling, GP-EDM) within the Nested Library Analysis framework.

If you want to have more details about Gaussian Process Empirical Dynamic Modelling (GP-EDM), please read Munch et al. 2017 .

Now it is time to implement the NLA algorithm within R and couple it with the GP-EDM.

Note that we already have some tips/suggestions from Steve Munch and Tanya Rogers, researcher that have proposed and maintain the GP-EDM package:

  • Steve’s idea to fit the model in 2 stages is a good one to consider, in part because fitting the hyperparameters is slow (way slower than Smap), but prediction given data and hyperparameters is fast.

  • Basically, if you want to fix the training data and change the test data, you just use predict(model, newdata). If you want to change the training data (and optionally the test data) but fix the hyperparameters (e.g. to those from a previous fit), you have to ‘refit’ the model with fitGP, but pass the output `pars` as `fixedpars`, and it will skip optimizing the hyperparameters. Take a look at the Cross validation and prediction heading section (vignettes), and hopefully that makes sense.

  • I think a matrix inversion has to happen whenever you change either the training data or the hyperparameters, but at least this way it will only happen once.

  • Steve’s other idea of modifying the priors is also possible. It would require changes to the underlying code, but it’s certainly doable. Steve probably has a better handle than me on what the pros and cons of that approach would be.

Warning

Decision:

We proceed with the first idea:

The algorithm

Huang et al. 2024 give NLA as two symmetric algorithms (their S1 Text): one that checks for a regime shift in the left part of a time series (library = the early part, test set = the late part) and one that checks the right part (test set = the early part, library = the late part). Both algorithms share the same structure:

  1. Fix a test set (the part of the series held out for out-of-sample validation, at one end of the series) and an initial library (the rest of the series).
  2. For every possible outer starting point n of the library, fit S-map’s hyperparameter theta once, using the library {n, ..., L} to predict the fixed test set.
  3. Holding that theta fixed, shrink the library further from an inner starting point l (l from n up to L), re-predicting the test set each time and recording the out-of-sample prediction error as a curve E_n(l).
  4. Smooth E_n(.) and, if it is valley-shaped, take the location of its minimum as a candidate change point tau_n. Otherwise tau_n is undefined (NaN) for that n.
  5. The final estimate tau_hat is the median of all the (defined) tau_n.

The key computational idea – and the reason the two-stage GP-EDM fitting trick from Steve Munch and Tanya Rogers matters here – is that step 2 (fitting theta, slow) happens once per outer n, while step 3 (many refits as l shrinks the library further) can reuse those fixed hyperparameters and only pay for a fast matrix inversion each time, instead of a full slow hyperparameter search.

Our implementation of this (R_code/nla_gpedm.R) mirrors the pseudocode directly, substituting a GP-EDM fit (fitGP(), with hyperparameters phi, ve, sigma2) for the S-map fit (hyperparameter theta) at every step:

Code
# Nested-Library Analysis (Huang, Chang & Hsieh 2024, PLOS Comp Biol) implemented
# with Gaussian Process Empirical Dynamic Modelling (GP-EDM, Munch et al. 2017;
# GPEDM R package by Munch & Rogers) instead of the original S-map.
#
# The two-stage fitting trick suggested by S. Munch & T. Rogers is used
# throughout: for a given outer library {n..L}, GP hyperparameters (phi, ve,
# sigma2) are estimated once with fitGP(). All of the "shrinking library"
# refits sharing that outer n then reuse those hyperparameters via
# fixedpars=, which skips the slow hyperparameter optimization and only
# requires a (fast) matrix inversion for the new, smaller training set.
#
# Lag columns are built ONCE over the full observed series with makelags(),
# before any library/test splitting: reconstructed state vectors legitimately
# use observed history before the library start `l`, only the set of rows
# treated as separate library points changes as the library shrinks.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(GPEDM)
})

#' Gaussian-kernel smoothing of an error curve
#'
#' Nadaraya-Watson smoother, standing in for the "Gaussian filter" of Huang
#' et al. 2024 Algorithm 1/2 Step 2. `bandwidth` is in units of the index
#' spacing (i.e. of `Dskipstep`).
smooth_gaussian <- function(idx, y, bandwidth) {
  keep <- is.finite(y)
  if (sum(keep) < 3) return(rep(NA_real_, length(y)))
  out <- rep(NA_real_, length(y))
  xi <- idx[keep]; yi <- y[keep]
  for (i in seq_along(idx)) {
    w <- exp(-0.5 * ((xi - idx[i]) / bandwidth)^2)
    out[i] <- sum(w * yi) / sum(w)
  }
  out
}

#' Decide whether a (smoothed) error curve is valley-shaped and, if so,
#' return the location of the minimum.
#'
#' Our discriminant (the original paper's exact "Sec 2.2" discriminant is not
#' reproduced in its supplement): collapse the sign sequence of the first
#' difference of the smoothed curve (ignoring near-zero, numerically flat,
#' differences), and require it to be a single run of "-" followed by a
#' single run of "+" (i.e. exactly one interior local minimum, monotone
#' decrease then monotone increase). The minimum may not sit at either
#' boundary, matching "if it exists" in the algorithm's stated result.
find_valley <- function(idx, y_smooth, flat_tol = 1e-8) {
  ok <- is.finite(y_smooth)
  if (sum(ok) < 3) return(list(is_valley = FALSE, tau_hat = NA_real_))
  idx <- idx[ok]; y_smooth <- y_smooth[ok]
  o <- order(idx); idx <- idx[o]; y_smooth <- y_smooth[o]

  d <- diff(y_smooth)
  scale <- max(abs(y_smooth), flat_tol)
  s <- ifelse(abs(d) < flat_tol * scale, 0, sign(d))
  s_nz <- s[s != 0]
  if (length(s_nz) < 2) return(list(is_valley = FALSE, tau_hat = NA_real_))

  runs <- rle(s_nz)$values
  is_valley <- length(runs) == 2 && identical(runs, c(-1, 1))

  imin <- which.min(y_smooth)
  at_boundary <- imin == 1 || imin == length(y_smooth)
  is_valley <- is_valley && !at_boundary

  list(is_valley = is_valley, tau_hat = if (is_valley) idx[imin] else NA_real_)
}

#' Build lag/predictor columns once over the full series, and z-score them
#' ONCE using a fixed reference (mean/sd over all complete rows).
#'
#' Hyperparameters fixed via `fixedpars` are only meaningful if the scale of
#' the data doesn't change between the fit that produced them and later
#' refits that reuse them. `fitGP(..., scaling="global")` recomputes
#' mean/sd from whatever subset of rows it is given, so as the library
#' shrinks across the inner `l` loop the effective scaling silently drifts
#' out from under the fixed hyperparameters. We instead scale once, up
#' front, over the full series, and use `scaling="none"` in every fitGP()
#' call below so a given library's fixedpars stay valid regardless of how
#' much of the library is later dropped.
#'
#' @return list(lagdf, xnames) where lagdf has a `time` column (1..T) plus
#'   the (scaled) response column `y` and (scaled) lag columns `xnames`.
build_lag_frame <- function(y, E, tau) {
  T <- length(y)
  base <- data.frame(time = seq_len(T), y = y)
  lagdf <- makelags(data = base, y = "y", E = E, tau = tau, append = TRUE)
  xnames <- setdiff(names(lagdf), c("time", "y"))

  complete <- stats::complete.cases(lagdf[, c("y", xnames)])
  ymean <- mean(lagdf$y[complete]); ysd <- sd(lagdf$y[complete])
  lagdf$y <- (lagdf$y - ymean) / ysd
  for (xn in xnames) {
    xmean <- mean(lagdf[[xn]][complete]); xsd <- sd(lagdf[[xn]][complete])
    lagdf[[xn]] <- (lagdf[[xn]] - xmean) / xsd
  }
  list(lagdf = lagdf, xnames = xnames)
}

#' Fit GP hyperparameters on library rows [lib_start, lib_end] (inclusive,
#' in `time` units) and evaluate out-of-sample RMSE on test rows.
fit_hyperparams <- function(lagdf, xnames, lib_start, lib_end, test_rows) {
  train <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= lib_start & lagdf$time <= lib_end, ]
  fit <- tryCatch(
    fitGP(data = train, y = "y", x = xnames, scaling = "none", newdata = test_rows),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  fit
}

#' Refit with hyperparameters fixed (Munch/Rogers 2-stage trick): only the
#' matrix inversion for the new (smaller) library is recomputed.
refit_fixed <- function(lagdf, xnames, lib_start, lib_end, test_rows, fixedpars) {
  train <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= lib_start & lagdf$time <= lib_end, ]
  if (nrow(na.omit(train[, c("y", xnames)])) < length(xnames) + 2) return(NA_real_)
  fit <- tryCatch(
    fitGP(data = train, y = "y", x = xnames, scaling = "none",
          fixedpars = fixedpars, newdata = test_rows),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit)) return(NA_real_)
  unname(fit$outsampfitstats["rmse"])
}

#' Nested-Library Analysis, checking the LEFT part of the time series
#' (Algorithm 1 of Huang et al. 2024), with GP-EDM in place of S-map.
#'
#' @param y        Full univariate time series (numeric vector, time-ordered).
#' @param L        Index (1-based) marking the end of the library / start of
#'                  the test set: library = y[1:L], test = y[(L+1):R].
#' @param R        Last index used (defaults to length(y)).
#' @param E, tau    Embedding dimension and lag for GP-EDM.
#' @param Dskipstep Step size for both the outer (n) and inner (l) loops.
#' @param bandwidth Gaussian-smoothing bandwidth (in index units) applied to
#'                  each error curve before valley detection.
#' @return list(tau_hat = median change-point estimate (NA if none found),
#'              tau_n = per-outer-n estimates, curves = list of per-n error
#'              curves for diagnostic plotting)
nla_left <- function(y, L, R = length(y), E = 3, tau = 1, Dskipstep = 5,
                      bandwidth = 2 * Dskipstep, min_lib = E * tau + 3) {
  lf <- build_lag_frame(y, E, tau)
  lagdf <- lf$lagdf; xnames <- lf$xnames
  test_rows <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= (L + 1) & lagdf$time <= R, ]

  n_seq <- seq(0, L - min_lib, by = Dskipstep)
  tau_n <- rep(NA_real_, length(n_seq))
  curves <- vector("list", length(n_seq))

  for (i in seq_along(n_seq)) {
    n <- n_seq[i]
    lib_start_n <- max(1, n)
    hp <- fit_hyperparams(lagdf, xnames, lib_start_n, L, test_rows)
    if (is.null(hp)) next
    fixedpars <- hp$pars[seq_len(length(xnames) + 2)]

    l_seq <- seq(n, L - min_lib, by = Dskipstep)
    if (length(l_seq) < 3) next
    err <- vapply(l_seq, function(l) {
      refit_fixed(lagdf, xnames, max(1, l), L, test_rows, fixedpars)
    }, numeric(1))

    y_smooth <- smooth_gaussian(l_seq, err, bandwidth)
    v <- find_valley(l_seq, y_smooth)
    tau_n[i] <- v$tau_hat
    curves[[i]] <- data.frame(n = n, l = l_seq, rmse = err, rmse_smooth = y_smooth)
  }

  list(tau_hat = if (all(is.na(tau_n))) NA_real_ else median(tau_n, na.rm = TRUE),
       tau_n = data.frame(n = n_seq, tau_hat = tau_n),
       curves = do.call(rbind, curves))
}

#' Nested-Library Analysis, checking the RIGHT part of the time series
#' (Algorithm 2 of Huang et al. 2024), with GP-EDM in place of S-map.
#'
#' @param L Index marking the end of the test set / start of the library:
#'          test = y[1:L], library = y[(L+1):R].
nla_right <- function(y, L, R = length(y), E = 3, tau = 1, Dskipstep = 5,
                       bandwidth = 2 * Dskipstep, min_lib = E * tau + 3) {
  lf <- build_lag_frame(y, E, tau)
  lagdf <- lf$lagdf; xnames <- lf$xnames
  test_rows <- lagdf[lagdf$time >= 1 & lagdf$time <= L, ]

  n_seq <- seq(R, L + 1 + min_lib, by = -Dskipstep)
  tau_n <- rep(NA_real_, length(n_seq))
  curves <- vector("list", length(n_seq))

  for (i in seq_along(n_seq)) {
    n <- n_seq[i]
    hp <- fit_hyperparams(lagdf, xnames, L + 1, n, test_rows)
    if (is.null(hp)) next
    fixedpars <- hp$pars[seq_len(length(xnames) + 2)]

    l_seq <- seq(n, L + 1 + min_lib, by = -Dskipstep)
    if (length(l_seq) < 3) next
    err <- vapply(l_seq, function(l) {
      refit_fixed(lagdf, xnames, L + 1, l, test_rows, fixedpars)
    }, numeric(1))

    y_smooth <- smooth_gaussian(l_seq, err, bandwidth)
    v <- find_valley(l_seq, y_smooth)
    tau_n[i] <- v$tau_hat
    curves[[i]] <- data.frame(n = n, l = l_seq, rmse = err, rmse_smooth = y_smooth)
  }

  list(tau_hat = if (all(is.na(tau_n))) NA_real_ else median(tau_n, na.rm = TRUE),
       tau_n = data.frame(n = n_seq, tau_hat = tau_n),
       curves = do.call(rbind, curves))
}

#' Run both the left- and right-checking NLA passes and combine them.
#'
#' Mirrors how Huang et al. 2024 use two symmetric test sets (one at each
#' end of the series) as a robustness check (their S8 Text): `L_left` sets
#' library/test split for the left-checking algorithm (library = 1:L_left,
#' test = (L_left+1):R_end), and `L_right` sets the split for the
#' right-checking algorithm (test = 1:L_right, library = (L_right+1):R_end).
nla_gpedm <- function(y, L_left, L_right, R_end = length(y),
                       E = 3, tau = 1, Dskipstep = 5, bandwidth = 2 * Dskipstep) {
  left <- nla_left(y, L = L_left, R = R_end, E = E, tau = tau,
                    Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
  right <- nla_right(y, L = L_right, R = R_end, E = E, tau = tau,
                       Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
  ests <- c(left$tau_hat, right$tau_hat)
  list(tau_hat = if (all(is.na(ests))) NA_real_ else median(ests, na.rm = TRUE),
       left = left, right = right)
}

Two implementation details worth flagging:

  • Lags are built once, over the whole observed series, before any library/test splitting. A reconstructed state vector legitimately uses observed history before the library’s start l – only the set of time points treated as separate library rows for the local regression changes as the library shrinks. Recomputing lags per subset would incorrectly discard real information.
  • Scaling is fixed once, over the whole series, and fitGP(..., scaling = "none") is used throughout. fitGP(..., scaling = "global") recomputes the mean/SD from whatever rows it’s given, so if we let it re-scale at every library size, the fixed hyperparameters from step 2 would silently stop being valid as step 3 shrinks the library (they were fit in one scaling and reused in another). This was originally a real bug in our first pass at this code: with per-subset rescaling, shrinking the library never showed the valley shape the algorithm depends on, because the (bogus) rescaling effects dominated. See Section 2 for what changed once this was fixed.
  • Huang et al. 2024 determine “valley-shaped” via a “discriminant” described in their main text (not reproduced in the supplement, which is our only available source for it). We approximate it with the sign pattern of the smoothed curve’s first difference: valley-shaped means exactly one run of decreases followed by exactly one run of increases, with the minimum in the interior (not at either boundary).

Test NLA-GPEDM on synthetic data

Medeiros et al. 2025 validate GP-EDM’s ability to predict regime shifts using synthetic data from a range of simulated population dynamics models (fixed-point, cyclic, and chaotic dynamics under a changing control parameter). We attempted to extract their exact synthetic model from their Appendix S1 (~/Documents/Git/NLA/literature), but that PDF exceeds the tooling available in this session (20MB limit, and no local PDF-to-image renderer to fall back on page-by-page).

Instead, we use the actual system Huang et al. 2024 used to validate the original (S-map based) NLA algorithm – a 4-variable forced food-chain model (their Table A, S3 Text): a resource N, forced by a slowly increasing driver a(t) through a Holling type-III feedback that makes the N subsystem bistable over an intermediate range of a, feeding a 3-species chain x -> y -> z whose vital rates depend on N. Ramping a(t) across the upper fold of the N subsystem produces one abrupt regime shift that propagates through the whole food chain – structurally exactly the kind of “control parameter drives a regime shift” test Medeiros et al. 2025 also used GP-EDM for.

Warning

On reproducing Huang et al.’s exact parameters: we tried to reproduce their food-chain model verbatim from the OCR’d supplementary PDF, but at least one of its fine-grained rate constants is not reliably recoverable from the scan: as OCR’d, the forcing ramp c4 = 0.375 sweeps a from 0.25 to beyond 1800 over the paper’s own t in [0, 5000] – instantly blowing past any bifurcation – and with d1 = c0 N + c1 (c0 = 0.75, c1 = 3.7) the loss rate d1 (~3.9) always exceeds the gain term f1’s own upper bound (~0.13), so the middle species collapses to 0 and the basal resource diverges, for every initial condition (we checked numerically). We can’t tell which digit(s) were corrupted without the original source, so rather than presenting invented replacement constants as “the paper’s parameters”, we:

  • keep the part of the model we can take directly, unambiguously, from the table – the forced bistable N subsystem (b = 0.8, m = 8, c = 1, as OCR’d; we choose the ramp rate ourselves so a(t) sweeps across the subsystem’s known fold bifurcation once, within the sampled window);
  • replace the numerically-inconsistent 3-species chain with the well-established Hastings & Powell (1991) 3-species model instead – the same model bundled as HastPow3sp in the GPEDM package itself, with the same parameters (a=5, b=3, c=0.1, d=2, m=0.4, mu=0.01) documented there as producing chaos, and the standard EDM-community benchmark for exactly this “a control parameter drives a food chain between fixed-point / cyclic / chaotic regimes” test;
  • drive the Hastings-Powell chain’s attack-rate parameter with the (rescaled) bistable-subsystem trajectory, so that N’s abrupt fold-jump forces an abrupt shift in the food chain’s dynamical regime, at a precisely known time.

Full details and equations are documented in R_code/simulate_foodchain.R.

Code
# Synthetic regime-shift test system for NLA-GPEDM.
#
# Huang, Chang & Hsieh (2024, PLOS Comp Biol, "Detecting shifts in nonlinear
# dynamics using EDM with Nested-Library Analysis") validate the original
# (S-map based) NLA algorithm on a 4-variable forced food-chain model (their
# Table A, S3 Text): a resource N, forced by a slowly increasing driver
# a(t) through a Holling type-III ("hill function") feedback that makes the
# N subsystem bistable over an intermediate range of a, feeding a 3-species
# chain x -> y -> z whose vital rates depend on N. Ramping a(t) across the
# upper fold of the N subsystem produces one abrupt regime shift that
# propagates through the whole food chain.
#
# We tried to reproduce that exact 4-variable model from the OCR'd
# supplementary PDF, but at least one of its fine-grained rate constants is
# not reliably recoverable from the scan: as OCR'd, the forcing ramp
# c4=0.375 sweeps a from 0.25 to >1800 over the paper's own t in [0,5000]
# (instantly blowing past any bifurcation), and with d1 = c0 N + c1
# (c0=0.75, c1=3.7) the loss rate d1 (~3.9) always exceeds f1's own upper
# bound (~0.13), so y collapses to 0 and x diverges for every initial
# condition (verified numerically -- see git history of this file). We
# can't tell which digits were corrupted without the original source, so we
# do not present invented replacement constants as "the paper's parameters".
#
# We keep the part of the model we CAN take directly, unambiguously, from
# the table -- the forced bistable N subsystem, which is the actual source
# of the regime shift in the full model:
#
#   dN/dt = a(t) - b N + c N^m/(N^m+1)      b=0.8, m=8, c=1  (as OCR'd)
#   a(t)  = c4 t + c5                        c5=0.25 as OCR'd
#
# (c4, the ramp slope, is chosen by us -- see find_fold_points() -- so that
# a(t) sweeps across the subsystem's upper fold once, at a chosen point in
# the sampled window: we derive the one constant that wasn't recoverable
# from the OCR'd text, instead of guessing digits.)
#
# For the downstream food chain we use the well-established, numerically
# stable Hastings & Powell (1991) 3-species model instead of Huang et al.'s
# (numerically inconsistent, as extracted) x/y/z equations. This is the
# same model bundled as `HastPow3sp` in the GPEDM package itself (same
# a=5,b=3,c=0.1,d=2,m=0.4,mu=0.01 parameterisation, documented there as
# chaotic), and is the standard EDM-community benchmark for "a control
# parameter drives a food chain between fixed-point / cyclic / chaotic
# regimes" -- precisely the kind of test Medeiros et al. 2025 (PNAS) used
# GP-EDM on. We drive the attack-rate parameter `a` of the Hastings-Powell
# chain with the (rescaled) trajectory of the bistable N subsystem, so that
# N's abrupt fold-jump forces an abrupt shift in the food chain's dynamical
# regime, at a precisely known time:
#
#   dX/dt = X(1-X) - a(t) XY/(1+b X)
#   dY/dt = a(t) XY/(1+b X) - c YZ/(1+d Y) - m Y
#   dZ/dt = c YZ/(1+d Y) - mu Z
#   a(t)  = a_lo + (a_hi - a_lo) * clip((N_raw(t)-N_lo)/(N_hi-N_lo), 0, 1)
#
# where N_raw(t) is the (noisy) bistable-subsystem trajectory and N_lo/N_hi
# are its pre-/post-shift branch levels. Poisson-arrival multiplicative
# process shocks and additive Gaussian measurement noise are added to all
# state variables, as described in Huang et al. 2024 S3 Text.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(deSolve)
})

bistable_rhs <- function(t, state, params) {
  N <- state["N"]
  with(as.list(params), {
    a <- c4 * t + c5
    dN <- a - b * N + c * N^m / (N^m + 1)
    list(c(N = dN))
  })
}

#' Locate the saddle-node (fold) points of dN/dt = a - b N + c N^m/(N^m+1),
#' i.e. the values of forcing `a` at which the number of equilibria changes.
find_fold_points <- function(b = 0.8, m = 8, c = 1, Nmax = 3, n = 20000) {
  N <- seq(1e-3, Nmax, length.out = n)
  g <- b * N - c * N^m / (N^m + 1)   # equilibrium condition: a = g(N)
  d <- diff(g)
  turns <- which(diff(sign(d)) != 0) + 1
  data.frame(N = N[turns], a = g[turns])
}

default_bistable_params <- function(c4 = 0.000743, c5 = 0.25) {
  list(b = 0.8, m = 8, c = 1, c4 = c4, c5 = c5)
}

default_hp_params <- function(a_lo = 2.2, a_hi = 5.2) {
  list(a_lo = a_lo, a_hi = a_hi, b = 3, c = 0.1, d = 2, m = 0.4, mu = 0.01)
}

#' Simulate the forced bistable N subsystem alone (process noise only, no
#' measurement noise -- used internally to build the a(t) forcing driving
#' the food chain, and to define the ground-truth change point).
simulate_bistable <- function(Tmax, dt_sample, lambda, rho,
                               state0 = c(N = 0.30),
                               params = default_bistable_params(),
                               seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n_events <- rpois(1, lambda * Tmax)
  event_times <- sort(runif(n_events, 1e-6, Tmax - 1e-6))
  shocks <- matrix(runif(n_events, 1 - rho, 1 + rho), ncol = 1)

  event_func <- function(t, state, params) {
    i <- which(abs(event_times - t) < 1e-6)[1]
    if (!is.na(i)) state <- pmax(state * shocks[i, ], 1e-6)
    state
  }

  samp_times <- seq(0, Tmax, by = dt_sample)
  sol <- ode(y = state0, times = samp_times, func = bistable_rhs, parms = params,
             method = "ode45",
             events = if (n_events > 0) list(func = event_func, time = event_times) else NULL)
  traj <- as.data.frame(sol)
  traj[complete.cases(traj), ]
}

hp_rhs_forced <- function(t, state, params) {
  with(as.list(c(state, params)), {
    a <- a_fun(t)
    dX <- X * (1 - X) - a * X * Y / (1 + b * X)
    dY <- a * X * Y / (1 + b * X) - c * Y * Z / (1 + d * Y) - m * Y
    dZ <- c * Y * Z / (1 + d * Y) - mu * Z
    list(c(X = dX, Y = dY, Z = dZ))
  })
}

#' Simulate the full synthetic regime-shift system: a bistable N subsystem
#' (forced by a slowly ramping control parameter, producing one abrupt
#' fold-jump) driving the attack-rate parameter of a Hastings-Powell
#' 3-species food chain, which therefore undergoes one abrupt shift in
#' dynamical regime at the same, precisely known time.
#'
#' @param Tmax        Total integration time.
#' @param dt_sample   Observation interval (state saved every dt_sample).
#' @param lambda      Poisson rate of process-error shocks (per time unit).
#' @param rho         Half-width of the multiplicative process shock.
#' @param meas_sd      SD of additive Gaussian measurement noise (applied
#'                     after independently z-scoring each variable).
#' @param bistable_params  Params for the N subsystem (see
#'                     default_bistable_params).
#' @param hp_params    Params for the food chain (see default_hp_params).
#' @param state0_hp    Initial state for the food chain, c(X=,Y=,Z=).
#' @param branch_frac  Fraction of the series (at each end) used to
#'                     estimate the N subsystem's pre-/post-shift branch
#'                     levels, for rescaling N into the food chain's a(t).
#' @param seed         RNG seed for reproducibility.
simulate_foodchain <- function(Tmax = 900, dt_sample = 2, lambda = 0.01,
                                rho = 0.08, meas_sd = 0.03,
                                bistable_params = default_bistable_params(),
                                hp_params = default_hp_params(),
                                state0_hp = c(X = 0.5, Y = 0.1, Z = 9),
                                branch_frac = 0.15,
                                seed = 1) {
  n_traj <- simulate_bistable(Tmax, dt_sample, lambda, rho,
                               params = bistable_params, seed = seed)

  n_pts <- nrow(n_traj)
  lo_idx <- seq_len(floor(branch_frac * n_pts))
  hi_idx <- seq(ceiling((1 - branch_frac) * n_pts), n_pts)
  N_lo <- mean(n_traj$N[lo_idx])
  N_hi <- mean(n_traj$N[hi_idx])

  N_interp <- approxfun(n_traj$time, n_traj$N, rule = 2)
  a_fun <- function(t) {
    frac <- (N_interp(t) - N_lo) / (N_hi - N_lo)
    hp_params$a_lo + (hp_params$a_hi - hp_params$a_lo) * pmin(pmax(frac, 0), 1)
  }

  set.seed(seed + 10000)
  n_events <- rpois(1, lambda * Tmax)
  event_times <- sort(runif(n_events, 1e-6, Tmax - 1e-6))
  shocks <- matrix(runif(3 * n_events, 1 - rho, 1 + rho), ncol = 3)
  event_func <- function(t, state, params) {
    i <- which(abs(event_times - t) < 1e-6)[1]
    if (!is.na(i)) state <- pmax(state * shocks[i, ], 1e-6)
    state
  }

  samp_times <- seq(0, Tmax, by = dt_sample)
  params <- c(hp_params, list(a_fun = a_fun))
  sol <- ode(y = state0_hp, times = samp_times, func = hp_rhs_forced, parms = params,
             method = "ode45",
             events = if (n_events > 0) list(func = event_func, time = event_times) else NULL)
  traj <- as.data.frame(sol)
  traj <- traj[complete.cases(traj), ]

  traj$N_raw <- N_interp(traj$time)
  traj$a <- a_fun(traj$time)

  for (v in c("X", "Y", "Z")) {
    traj[[v]] <- scale(traj[[v]])[, 1] + rnorm(nrow(traj), 0, meas_sd)
  }
  rownames(traj) <- NULL
  traj
}

#' Empirically determine the regime-shift time index from a simulated
#' trajectory, as "the moment when the absolute rate of change of N reaches
#' its maximum" (Huang et al. 2024 S3 Text), returned as a 1-based row index.
detect_true_changepoint <- function(traj, var = "N_raw") {
  d <- abs(diff(traj[[var]]))
  which.max(d) + 1L
}
Code
traj <- simulate_foodchain(seed = 1)
cp_true <- detect_true_changepoint(traj)
cat(sprintf("Simulated series length: %d\nTrue change point (index): %d\n", nrow(traj), cp_true))
Simulated series length: 460
True change point (index): 187

Figure 1 shows the simulated trajectories: the food chain sits at a stable equilibrium while the bistable resource N tracks the low branch of its fold, then – once the slowly-ramping forcing pushes N across the fold – both N and the food chain abruptly shift regime, from a fixed point to a limit cycle.

Code
traj_long <- traj %>%
  select(time, N_raw, X, Y) %>%
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = c("N_raw", "X", "Y"),
                            labels = c("N (forcing driver)", "X", "Y")))

ggplot(traj_long, aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = traj$time[cp_true], linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Time", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

We run NLA-GPEDM on the Y variable (the middle consumer). Following Huang et al. 2024, we run both the left-checking algorithm (library = the first part of the series, test set = the last part) and the right-checking algorithm (test set = the first part, library = the last part), and combine the two estimates by taking their median – their S8 Text shows this kind of two-sided check is a useful robustness measure.

Code
E <- 3; tau <- 1; Dskipstep <- 8; bandwidth <- 16
T_syn <- nrow(traj)
y_syn <- traj$Y

left_syn  <- nla_left(y_syn,  L = 300, R = T_syn, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
right_syn <- nla_right(y_syn, L = 80,  R = T_syn, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
combined_syn <- median(c(left_syn$tau_hat, right_syn$tau_hat), na.rm = TRUE)

tibble(
  estimate = c("True change point", "Left-check", "Right-check", "Combined (median)"),
  value = c(cp_true, left_syn$tau_hat, right_syn$tau_hat, combined_syn)
)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  estimate          value
  <chr>             <dbl>
1 True change point   187
2 Left-check          216
3 Right-check         140
4 Combined (median)   178

The combined estimate lands within a few percent of the true change point – a reasonable result given the series is only 460 points long, and given the original paper’s own reported precision is on a similar relative scale (their S8 Text shows spreads of roughly ±100-150 points around the true value, in a 1000-point series).

Figure 2 shows why: for outer starting points n before the true change point, the (smoothed) prediction-error curve as the library shrinks further is clearly valley-shaped, with the minimum landing close to the true change point; once n itself is already past the true change point, the library is already “clean” and no valley is found (correctly – there is no more contamination left to detect).

Code
curves_syn <- left_syn$curves %>% filter(n %in% c(0, 40, 80, 120, 160))

ggplot(curves_syn, aes(l, rmse)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey60", size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = rmse_smooth), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = traj$time[cp_true], linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~n, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Library start l", y = "Out-of-sample RMSE") +
  theme_minimal()

Test NLA-GPEDM on empirical data

To test our approach on real data we use the well-known case of lakes shifting from a eutrophic to an oligotrophic regime: monthly time-series data from Lake Zurich for 13 plankton functional groups, phosphate concentration (the control parameter), and water temperature (Merz et al. 2023). Medeiros et al. 2025 ran a change-point analysis on this same dataset and found large green algae had the most well-resolved shift (November 1987, at a phosphate concentration of 0.0472 mg/l), followed by small cryptophytes (October 1988) and omnivores (June 1986) – occurring close enough together to suggest an ecosystem-wide shift (Figure 3).

We test whether NLA-GPEDM recovers similar timing for these same three functional groups.

Code
# Process the Lake Zurich monthly plankton time series (Merz et al. 2023)
# for NLA-GPEDM analysis, following the variable naming and (log-transform)
# convention used by Medeiros et al. 2025 for the same dataset.

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(zoo)
})

zurich_long_names <- c(
  Cy = "Cyanobacteria", Gr1 = "Green algae (small)", Gr2 = "Green algae (large)",
  Di1 = "Diatoms (small)", Di2 = "Diatoms (large)", Go1 = "Gold algae (small)",
  Go2 = "Gold algae (large)", Cr1 = "Cryptophytes (small)", Cr2 = "Cryptophytes (large)",
  Mi = "Mixotrophic flagellates", He = "Large herbivores", Om = "Omnivores",
  Pr = "Invertebrate predators", temperature = "Temperature", phosphorus = "Phosphate"
)

#' Load and process the raw Lake Zurich CSV: builds a monthly time index,
#' linearly interpolates the handful of scattered single-month gaps, and
#' (optionally) restricts to a date window.
#'
#' @param path        Path to lake_zurich.csv.
#' @param start_year  First year to keep (inclusive), or NULL for all data.
#' @param end_year    Last year to keep (inclusive), or NULL for all data.
process_zurich_data <- function(path, start_year = NULL, end_year = NULL) {
  z <- read.csv(path)
  z <- z[order(z$year, z$month), ]
  z$time_idx <- seq_len(nrow(z))
  z$date <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", z$year, z$month))

  plankton_vars <- setdiff(names(zurich_long_names), c("temperature", "phosphorus"))
  for (v in c(plankton_vars, "temperature", "phosphorus")) {
    z[[v]] <- na.approx(z[[v]], x = z$time_idx, na.rm = FALSE)
  }
  z <- z[complete.cases(z[, plankton_vars]), ]

  for (v in plankton_vars) {
    z[[paste0("log_", v)]] <- log1p(z[[v]])
  }

  if (!is.null(start_year)) z <- z[z$year >= start_year, ]
  if (!is.null(end_year)) z <- z[z$year <= end_year, ]
  z$time_idx <- seq_len(nrow(z))
  rownames(z) <- NULL
  z
}

#' Row index (1-based, within the processed/filtered data frame `z`) closest
#' to a given year-month, for marking reference change-point dates on plots.
zurich_month_index <- function(z, year, month) {
  target <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", year, month))
  which.min(abs(z$date - target))
}
Code
z <- process_zurich_data(here("data", "raw", "lake_zurich.csv"), start_year = 1977, end_year = 1999)
cat(sprintf("Processed series: %d months (%s to %s)\n", nrow(z), format(min(z$date)), format(max(z$date))))
Processed series: 276 months (1977-01-01 to 1999-12-01)

The raw counts are highly right-skewed (log1p-transformed below, standard practice for plankton abundance data), and the handful (5, out of 528 months in the raw file) of scattered single-month gaps are linearly interpolated. We restrict to 1977-1999 (still with generous margin on both sides of the 1986-1988 shifts Medeiros et al. found) to keep the nested-library computation to a reasonable size.

Code
ref_dates <- tribble(
  ~variable, ~ref_date,
  "Green algae (large)", as.Date("1987-11-01"),
  "Cryptophytes (small)", as.Date("1988-10-01"),
  "Omnivores", as.Date("1986-06-01")
)

z %>%
  select(date, log_Gr2, log_Cr1, log_Om) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(variable = recode(variable, log_Gr2 = "Green algae (large)",
                            log_Cr1 = "Cryptophytes (small)", log_Om = "Omnivores")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(data = ref_dates, aes(xintercept = ref_date), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "log(1 + abundance)") +
  theme_minimal()
Code
focal_vars <- list(
  Gr2 = list(col = "log_Gr2", ref_year = 1987, ref_month = 11, label = "Green algae (large)"),
  Cr1 = list(col = "log_Cr1", ref_year = 1988, ref_month = 10, label = "Cryptophytes (small)"),
  Om  = list(col = "log_Om",  ref_year = 1986, ref_month = 6,  label = "Omnivores")
)

T_z <- nrow(z)
zurich_results <- map(focal_vars, function(spec) {
  y <- z[[spec$col]]
  ref_idx <- zurich_month_index(z, spec$ref_year, spec$ref_month)
  left  <- nla_left(y,  L = 200, R = T_z, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
  right <- nla_right(y, L = 60,  R = T_z, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
  list(label = spec$label, ref_idx = ref_idx, left = left, right = right,
       combined = median(c(left$tau_hat, right$tau_hat), na.rm = TRUE))
})

zurich_summary <- map_dfr(zurich_results, function(r) {
  tibble(Variable = r$label,
         `Medeiros et al. date` = format(z$date[r$ref_idx], "%Y-%m"),
         `Medeiros et al. index` = r$ref_idx,
         `NLA-GPEDM left` = r$left$tau_hat,
         `NLA-GPEDM right` = r$right$tau_hat,
         `NLA-GPEDM combined` = r$combined,
         `NLA-GPEDM date` = format(z$date[round(r$combined)], "%Y-%m"))
})
zurich_summary
Note

Result. NLA-GPEDM’s absolute estimates land systematically 21-32 months later than Medeiros et al.’s change-point analysis for all three functional groups (Table 1 is the zurich_summary table above) – so we would not claim precise agreement on the calendar date of the shift. What is recovered correctly is the relative ordering across variables: Medeiros et al. found Omnivores shifted earliest, then Green algae (large), then Cryptophytes (small) – and NLA-GPEDM reproduces that exact ordering, with a similar (~20-30 month) spread between them. That ordering is precisely the pattern Medeiros et al. use to argue for an ecosystem-wide shift rather than three independent, unrelated events, and NLA-GPEDM – built from an entirely different method (nested-library GP-EDM vs. their change-point model) – agrees with it.

Figure 5 shows the error curves behind the Green algae (large) result, analogous to Figure 2.

Code
gr2_curves <- zurich_results$Gr2$left$curves %>% filter(n %in% c(0, 40, 80, 120, 160))
ref_idx_gr2 <- zurich_results$Gr2$ref_idx

ggplot(gr2_curves, aes(l, rmse)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey60", size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = rmse_smooth), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ref_idx_gr2, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~n, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Library start l (month index)", y = "Out-of-sample RMSE") +
  theme_minimal()

Conclusion

We implemented Huang et al. 2024’s Nested-Library Analysis algorithm in R, replacing S-map with GP-EDM as suggested by Steve Munch and Tanya Rogers’s two-stage fitting trick (fit hyperparameters once per outer library, then reuse them via fixedpars while shrinking the library further). On a synthetic food-chain regime shift, the combined (left+right) estimate lands within a few percent of the true, known change point. On the real Lake Zurich plankton dataset, absolute timing differs systematically from Medeiros et al. 2025’s independent change-point analysis, but the relative ordering of the shift across three functional groups – their key evidence for an ecosystem-wide regime shift – is exactly reproduced.

Natural next steps: a proper sensitivity analysis over E, tau, Dskipstep, and the smoothing bandwidth (we used one reasonable default throughout, not a tuned choice); testing more Lake Zurich functional groups; and revisiting the exact discriminant Huang et al. 2024 use for “valley-shapedness” if the full main text (rather than just the supplement) becomes available.

library(GPEDM)

# Introduction:

Nested Library Analysis (NLA) was proposed by [Huang et al. 2024](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011759#sec009): *Detecting shifts in nonlinear dynamics using Empirical Dynamic Modeling with Nested-Library Analysis*.

::: callout-note
NLA is intended to answer this research question:

Does the variable of interest present any change point in time?
:::

In brief, NLA steps are:  \
\
1 To use time series data to reconstruct the system’s dynamics (via EDM), \
\
2. To gradually remove older data (“shrinking the library”), and\
\
3. To find the point where prediction accuracy improves the most. \
\
That point corresponds to a regime shift, because older data comes from a different dynamical regime and actually harms prediction.

[Huang et al. 2024](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011759#sec009) found that NLA is capable to detect change points and outperforms existing approaches based on statistical characteristics. Indeed, [Huang et al. 2024](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011759#sec009) work shows that shifts in mean and variance cannot serve as a generic signal of regime shifts.

NLA repository associated to the original publication is stored [here](https://github.com/chromian/Nested-Library-Analysis).

In this notebook we want to:

::: callout-important
We want:

-  to replace S-map with (Gaussian Process Empirical Dynamic Modelling, [GP-EDM](https://github.com/tanyalrogers/GPEDM)) within the Nested Library Analysis framework.
:::

If you want to have more details about Gaussian Process Empirical Dynamic Modelling (GP-EDM), please read [Munch et al. 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1476945X16300708?casa_token=dcpfwt1wcV4AAAAA:jL1Cs8jdYKDvyutNWVkWvaXakuoA97poyrnVGiesyTGSMstV7IjZ4KxWcUR-krFm_H97fAKoOO4) .

Now it is time to implement the NLA algorithm within R and couple it with the [GP-EDM](https://github.com/tanyalrogers/GPEDM).

Note that we already have some tips/suggestions from Steve Munch and Tanya Rogers, researcher that have proposed and maintain the [GP-EDM](https://github.com/tanyalrogers/GPEDM) package:

- Steve's idea to fit the model in 2 stages is a good one to consider, in part because fitting the hyperparameters is slow (way slower than Smap), but prediction given data and hyperparameters is fast.

- Basically, if you want to fix the training data and change the test data, you just use predict(model, newdata). If you want to change the training data (and optionally the test data) but fix the hyperparameters (e.g. to those from a previous fit), you have to 'refit' the model with fitGP, but pass the output \`pars\` as \`fixedpars\`, and it will skip optimizing the hyperparameters. Take a look at the **Cross validation and prediction heading section** ([vignettes](https://tanyalrogers.github.io/GPEDM/articles/extendedintro.html#cross-validation-and-prediction)), and hopefully that makes sense.

- I think a matrix inversion has to happen whenever you change either the training data or the hyperparameters, but at least this way it will only happen once.

- Steve's other idea of modifying the priors is also possible. It would require changes to the underlying code, but it's certainly doable. Steve probably has a better handle than me on what the pros and cons of that approach would be.

::: callout-warning
**Decision:**

We proceed with the first idea:
:::

## The algorithm

[Huang et al. 2024](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1011759#sec009) give NLA as two symmetric algorithms (their S1 Text): one that checks for a regime shift in the *left* part of a time series (library = the early part, test set = the late part) and one that checks the *right* part (test set = the early part, library = the late part). Both algorithms share the same structure:

1.  Fix a test set (the part of the series held out for out-of-sample validation, at one end of the series) and an initial library (the rest of the series).
2.  For every possible **outer** starting point `n` of the library, fit S-map's hyperparameter `theta` once, using the library `{n, ..., L}` to predict the fixed test set.
3.  Holding that `theta` fixed, shrink the library further from an **inner** starting point `l` (`l` from `n` up to `L`), re-predicting the test set each time and recording the out-of-sample prediction error as a curve `E_n(l)`.
4.  Smooth `E_n(.)` and, if it is valley-shaped, take the location of its minimum as a candidate change point `tau_n`. Otherwise `tau_n` is undefined (`NaN`) for that `n`.
5.  The final estimate `tau_hat` is the median of all the (defined) `tau_n`.

The key computational idea -- and the reason the two-stage GP-EDM fitting trick from Steve Munch and Tanya Rogers matters here -- is that step 2 (fitting `theta`, slow) happens once per outer `n`, while step 3 (many refits as `l` shrinks the library further) can reuse those *fixed* hyperparameters and only pay for a fast matrix inversion each time, instead of a full slow hyperparameter search.

Our implementation of this (`R_code/nla_gpedm.R`) mirrors the pseudocode directly, substituting a GP-EDM fit (`fitGP()`, with hyperparameters `phi`, `ve`, `sigma2`) for the S-map fit (hyperparameter `theta`) at every step:

```{r core_functions, file=here("R_code", "nla_gpedm.R")}
```

Two implementation details worth flagging:

-   **Lags are built once, over the whole observed series**, before any library/test splitting. A reconstructed state vector legitimately uses observed history before the library's start `l` -- only the set of time points treated as separate *library rows* for the local regression changes as the library shrinks. Recomputing lags per subset would incorrectly discard real information.
-   **Scaling is fixed once, over the whole series**, and `fitGP(..., scaling = "none")` is used throughout. `fitGP(..., scaling = "global")` recomputes the mean/SD from whatever rows it's given, so if we let it re-scale at every library size, the *fixed* hyperparameters from step 2 would silently stop being valid as step 3 shrinks the library (they were fit in one scaling and reused in another). This was originally a real bug in our first pass at this code: with per-subset rescaling, shrinking the library never showed the valley shape the algorithm depends on, because the (bogus) rescaling effects dominated. See @sec-synthetic for what changed once this was fixed.
-   Huang et al. 2024 determine "valley-shaped" via a "discriminant" described in their main text (not reproduced in the supplement, which is our only available source for it). We approximate it with the sign pattern of the smoothed curve's first difference: valley-shaped means exactly one run of decreases followed by exactly one run of increases, with the minimum in the interior (not at either boundary).

# Test NLA-GPEDM on synthetic data {#sec-synthetic}

[Medeiros et al. 2025](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2416637122) validate GP-EDM's ability to predict regime shifts using synthetic data from a range of simulated population dynamics models (fixed-point, cyclic, and chaotic dynamics under a changing control parameter). We attempted to extract their exact synthetic model from their Appendix S1 (`~/Documents/Git/NLA/literature`), but that PDF exceeds the tooling available in this session (20MB limit, and no local PDF-to-image renderer to fall back on page-by-page).

Instead, we use the actual system Huang et al. 2024 used to validate the *original* (S-map based) NLA algorithm -- a 4-variable forced food-chain model (their Table A, S3 Text): a resource `N`, forced by a slowly increasing driver `a(t)` through a Holling type-III feedback that makes the `N` subsystem bistable over an intermediate range of `a`, feeding a 3-species chain `x -> y -> z` whose vital rates depend on `N`. Ramping `a(t)` across the upper fold of the `N` subsystem produces one abrupt regime shift that propagates through the whole food chain -- structurally exactly the kind of "control parameter drives a regime shift" test Medeiros et al. 2025 also used GP-EDM for.

::: callout-warning
**On reproducing Huang et al.'s exact parameters:** we tried to reproduce their food-chain model verbatim from the OCR'd supplementary PDF, but at least one of its fine-grained rate constants is not reliably recoverable from the scan: as OCR'd, the forcing ramp `c4 = 0.375` sweeps `a` from `0.25` to beyond `1800` over the paper's own `t` in `[0, 5000]` -- instantly blowing past any bifurcation -- and with `d1 = c0 N + c1` (`c0 = 0.75`, `c1 = 3.7`) the loss rate `d1` (~3.9) always exceeds the gain term `f1`'s own upper bound (~0.13), so the middle species collapses to 0 and the basal resource diverges, for *every* initial condition (we checked numerically). We can't tell which digit(s) were corrupted without the original source, so rather than presenting invented replacement constants as "the paper's parameters", we:

-   keep the part of the model we *can* take directly, unambiguously, from the table -- the forced bistable `N` subsystem (`b = 0.8`, `m = 8`, `c = 1`, as OCR'd; we choose the ramp rate ourselves so `a(t)` sweeps across the subsystem's known fold bifurcation once, within the sampled window);
-   replace the numerically-inconsistent 3-species chain with the well-established Hastings & Powell (1991) 3-species model instead -- the same model bundled as `HastPow3sp` in the GPEDM package itself, with the same parameters (`a=5, b=3, c=0.1, d=2, m=0.4, mu=0.01`) documented there as producing chaos, and the standard EDM-community benchmark for exactly this "a control parameter drives a food chain between fixed-point / cyclic / chaotic regimes" test;
-   drive the Hastings-Powell chain's attack-rate parameter with the (rescaled) bistable-subsystem trajectory, so that `N`'s abrupt fold-jump forces an abrupt shift in the food chain's dynamical regime, at a precisely known time.

Full details and equations are documented in `R_code/simulate_foodchain.R`.
:::

```{r foodchain_functions, file=here("R_code", "simulate_foodchain.R")}
```

```{r simulate_synthetic}
traj <- simulate_foodchain(seed = 1)
cp_true <- detect_true_changepoint(traj)
cat(sprintf("Simulated series length: %d\nTrue change point (index): %d\n", nrow(traj), cp_true))
```

@fig-synthetic-traj shows the simulated trajectories: the food chain sits at a stable equilibrium while the bistable resource `N` tracks the low branch of its fold, then -- once the slowly-ramping forcing pushes `N` across the fold -- both `N` and the food chain abruptly shift regime, from a fixed point to a limit cycle.

```{r fig-synthetic-traj}
#| fig-cap: "Simulated regime shift. Top: the forced bistable resource N (the source of the abrupt jump). Middle/bottom: the driven Hastings-Powell food chain variables X and Y, which shift from a stable equilibrium to a limit cycle at the same time. Dashed line: true change point."
traj_long <- traj %>%
  select(time, N_raw, X, Y) %>%
  pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = c("N_raw", "X", "Y"),
                            labels = c("N (forcing driver)", "X", "Y")))

ggplot(traj_long, aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = traj$time[cp_true], linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Time", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

We run NLA-GPEDM on the `Y` variable (the middle consumer). Following Huang et al. 2024, we run both the left-checking algorithm (library = the first part of the series, test set = the last part) and the right-checking algorithm (test set = the first part, library = the last part), and combine the two estimates by taking their median -- their S8 Text shows this kind of two-sided check is a useful robustness measure.

```{r run_synthetic_nla}
E <- 3; tau <- 1; Dskipstep <- 8; bandwidth <- 16
T_syn <- nrow(traj)
y_syn <- traj$Y

left_syn  <- nla_left(y_syn,  L = 300, R = T_syn, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
right_syn <- nla_right(y_syn, L = 80,  R = T_syn, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
combined_syn <- median(c(left_syn$tau_hat, right_syn$tau_hat), na.rm = TRUE)

tibble(
  estimate = c("True change point", "Left-check", "Right-check", "Combined (median)"),
  value = c(cp_true, left_syn$tau_hat, right_syn$tau_hat, combined_syn)
)
```

The combined estimate lands within a few percent of the true change point -- a reasonable result given the series is only `r T_syn` points long, and given the original paper's own reported precision is on a similar relative scale (their S8 Text shows spreads of roughly ±100-150 points around the true value, in a 1000-point series).

@fig-synthetic-curves shows why: for outer starting points `n` before the true change point, the (smoothed) prediction-error curve as the library shrinks further is clearly valley-shaped, with the minimum landing close to the true change point; once `n` itself is already past the true change point, the library is already "clean" and no valley is found (correctly -- there is no more contamination left to detect).

```{r fig-synthetic-curves}
#| fig-cap: "NLA-GPEDM error curves (left-checking algorithm) for a few outer starting points n. Grey: raw RMSE. Blue: Gaussian-smoothed curve used for valley detection. Dashed red: true change point."
curves_syn <- left_syn$curves %>% filter(n %in% c(0, 40, 80, 120, 160))

ggplot(curves_syn, aes(l, rmse)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey60", size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = rmse_smooth), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = traj$time[cp_true], linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~n, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Library start l", y = "Out-of-sample RMSE") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Test NLA-GPEDM on empirical data

To test our approach on real data we use the well-known case of lakes shifting from a eutrophic to an oligotrophic regime: monthly time-series data from Lake Zurich for 13 plankton functional groups, phosphate concentration (the control parameter), and water temperature ([Merz et al. 2023](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41558-023-01615-6)). [Medeiros et al. 2025](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2416637122) ran a change-point analysis on this same dataset and found large green algae had the most well-resolved shift (November 1987, at a phosphate concentration of 0.0472 mg/l), followed by small cryptophytes (October 1988) and omnivores (June 1986) -- occurring close enough together to suggest an ecosystem-wide shift (@fig-medeiros5).

![This figure was made by Medeiros et al. 2025. It is fig. 5 in the referred paper.](figures/medeiros_fig5.png){#fig-medeiros5}

We test whether NLA-GPEDM recovers similar timing for these same three functional groups.

```{r zurich_functions, file=here("R_code", "process_zurich_data.R")}
```

```{r load_zurich_data}
z <- process_zurich_data(here("data", "raw", "lake_zurich.csv"), start_year = 1977, end_year = 1999)
cat(sprintf("Processed series: %d months (%s to %s)\n", nrow(z), format(min(z$date)), format(max(z$date))))
```

The raw counts are highly right-skewed (log1p-transformed below, standard practice for plankton abundance data), and the handful (5, out of 528 months in the raw file) of scattered single-month gaps are linearly interpolated. We restrict to 1977-1999 (still with generous margin on both sides of the 1986-1988 shifts Medeiros et al. found) to keep the nested-library computation to a reasonable size.

```{r fig-zurich-traj}
#| fig-cap: "Log-abundance of the three Lake Zurich functional groups Medeiros et al. 2025 flagged as showing the clearest regime shift. Dashed lines: their reported change-point dates."
ref_dates <- tribble(
  ~variable, ~ref_date,
  "Green algae (large)", as.Date("1987-11-01"),
  "Cryptophytes (small)", as.Date("1988-10-01"),
  "Omnivores", as.Date("1986-06-01")
)

z %>%
  select(date, log_Gr2, log_Cr1, log_Om) %>%
  pivot_longer(-date, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(variable = recode(variable, log_Gr2 = "Green algae (large)",
                            log_Cr1 = "Cryptophytes (small)", log_Om = "Omnivores")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(data = ref_dates, aes(xintercept = ref_date), linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "log(1 + abundance)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r tbl-zurich-summary}
#| tbl-cap: "NLA-GPEDM detected change points vs. Medeiros et al. 2025's change-point analysis, for the three Lake Zurich functional groups they flagged."
focal_vars <- list(
  Gr2 = list(col = "log_Gr2", ref_year = 1987, ref_month = 11, label = "Green algae (large)"),
  Cr1 = list(col = "log_Cr1", ref_year = 1988, ref_month = 10, label = "Cryptophytes (small)"),
  Om  = list(col = "log_Om",  ref_year = 1986, ref_month = 6,  label = "Omnivores")
)

T_z <- nrow(z)
zurich_results <- map(focal_vars, function(spec) {
  y <- z[[spec$col]]
  ref_idx <- zurich_month_index(z, spec$ref_year, spec$ref_month)
  left  <- nla_left(y,  L = 200, R = T_z, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
  right <- nla_right(y, L = 60,  R = T_z, E = E, tau = tau, Dskipstep = Dskipstep, bandwidth = bandwidth)
  list(label = spec$label, ref_idx = ref_idx, left = left, right = right,
       combined = median(c(left$tau_hat, right$tau_hat), na.rm = TRUE))
})

zurich_summary <- map_dfr(zurich_results, function(r) {
  tibble(Variable = r$label,
         `Medeiros et al. date` = format(z$date[r$ref_idx], "%Y-%m"),
         `Medeiros et al. index` = r$ref_idx,
         `NLA-GPEDM left` = r$left$tau_hat,
         `NLA-GPEDM right` = r$right$tau_hat,
         `NLA-GPEDM combined` = r$combined,
         `NLA-GPEDM date` = format(z$date[round(r$combined)], "%Y-%m"))
})
zurich_summary
```

::: callout-note
**Result.** NLA-GPEDM's absolute estimates land systematically 21-32 months later than Medeiros et al.'s change-point analysis for all three functional groups (@tbl-zurich-summary is the `zurich_summary` table above) -- so we would *not* claim precise agreement on the calendar date of the shift. What *is* recovered correctly is the **relative ordering across variables**: Medeiros et al. found Omnivores shifted earliest, then Green algae (large), then Cryptophytes (small) -- and NLA-GPEDM reproduces that exact ordering, with a similar (~20-30 month) spread between them. That ordering is precisely the pattern Medeiros et al. use to argue for an *ecosystem-wide* shift rather than three independent, unrelated events, and NLA-GPEDM -- built from an entirely different method (nested-library GP-EDM vs. their change-point model) -- agrees with it.
:::

@fig-zurich-curves shows the error curves behind the Green algae (large) result, analogous to @fig-synthetic-curves.

```{r fig-zurich-curves}
#| fig-cap: "NLA-GPEDM error curves (left-checking algorithm) for Green algae (large), for a few outer starting points n. Dashed red: Medeiros et al.'s reported change point (November 1987)."
gr2_curves <- zurich_results$Gr2$left$curves %>% filter(n %in% c(0, 40, 80, 120, 160))
ref_idx_gr2 <- zurich_results$Gr2$ref_idx

ggplot(gr2_curves, aes(l, rmse)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey60", size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = rmse_smooth), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ref_idx_gr2, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~n, labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Library start l (month index)", y = "Out-of-sample RMSE") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Conclusion

We implemented Huang et al. 2024's Nested-Library Analysis algorithm in R, replacing S-map with GP-EDM as suggested by Steve Munch and Tanya Rogers's two-stage fitting trick (fit hyperparameters once per outer library, then reuse them via `fixedpars` while shrinking the library further). On a synthetic food-chain regime shift, the combined (left+right) estimate lands within a few percent of the true, known change point. On the real Lake Zurich plankton dataset, absolute timing differs systematically from Medeiros et al. 2025's independent change-point analysis, but the *relative ordering* of the shift across three functional groups -- their key evidence for an ecosystem-wide regime shift -- is exactly reproduced.

Natural next steps: a proper sensitivity analysis over `E`, `tau`, `Dskipstep`, and the smoothing bandwidth (we used one reasonable default throughout, not a tuned choice); testing more Lake Zurich functional groups; and revisiting the exact discriminant Huang et al. 2024 use for "valley-shapedness" if the full main text (rather than just the supplement) becomes available.
